prompt: In a bar chart of orders by region, what is the mark?

choices.text: The length of each bar
choices.why: That is the channel: the property of the mark that changes with the number.

choices.text: The axis along the bottom
choices.why: The axis is the ruler the lengths are read against. It is not drawn once per region.

choices.text: Each bar
choices.why: Right. The mark is the thing drawn once per item of data, and there is one bar per region.

choices.text: The number of orders
choices.why: That is the data. The mark is what the chart draws to stand for it.

prompt: What is a channel, in the sense this course uses the word?

choices.text: A property of a mark that changes with the data, such as its position or colour
choices.why: Right. Bertin called the same idea a visual variable.

choices.text: The column of the table that a chart's numbers are drawn from
choices.why: A column is data. A channel is how a column is shown.

choices.text: The software that draws the chart
choices.why: Channels are the same in every tool; that is why the idea has lasted sixty years.

choices.text: A series of related charts placed side by side
choices.why: That is small multiples, the subject of lesson 10.

prompt: A bar chart's axis starts at 70,000 instead of zero. Which link has it broken?

choices.text: Between the bars and their categories
choices.why: Each bar still sits beside its region's name. The names are fine; the lengths are not.

choices.text: Between each bar's length and its number
choices.why: Right. A bar whose number is twice another's is no longer twice as long, so the channel lies.

choices.text: Between the colour and the legend
choices.why: There is no colour channel in play here, only length.

choices.text: None; it only makes small differences easier to see
choices.why: It does make them bigger, and that is exactly the problem: bigger than they are.

prompt: A chart draws correctly, with no software errors, and still misleads its reader. Which explanation fits best?

choices.text: The data must have been wrong
choices.why: The data can be perfect and the chart still mislead, as a truncated axis shows.

choices.text: The reader did not look carefully enough
choices.why: A chart is read in a glance. One that needs careful reading to avoid a wrong conclusion has failed.

choices.text: The chart had too many colours
choices.why: That can make a chart hard to read, but a one-colour chart misleads just as easily.

choices.text: A channel was chosen that says something the data does not
choices.why: Right. The software draws what it is told; the mistake is in what it was told to draw.

prompt: Of the six panels that drew the same five numbers, in which two could you best say by how much one region beats another?

choices.text: Position and length
choices.why: Right. Both are read as a distance from a common start, which the eye judges precisely.

choices.text: Angle and area
choices.why: These showed which was largest and left the amounts to a guess.

choices.text: Lightness and hue
choices.why: Lightness kept only the order, and hue lost even that.

choices.text: Length and lightness
choices.why: Length was one of them, but lightness gives an order and no amounts.

prompt: Southeast had 77,567 orders and North 11,852. How many times North's area should Southeast's circle have, to one decimal place?
hint: Area is the channel, so the areas keep the ratio of the numbers.

prompt: Readers looked at the area panel and judged the largest circle to be three or four times the smallest. What does that show about area?

choices.text: The circles were drawn with the wrong sizes
choices.why: They were sized correctly by area. The error is in the reading, not the drawing.

choices.text: Area is read more precisely than length
choices.why: The opposite: the bars in the length panel were read far more accurately.

choices.text: Circles should be sized by their radius instead
choices.why: Sizing by radius would make the largest circle about 43 times the smallest in area, a far worse lie.

choices.text: The eye underestimates differences in area
choices.why: Right. The real ratio was about 6.5, and lesson 2 explains why area reads short.

prompt: A colleague wants each region's orders shown as a different shape on a chart. What will the reader be able to tell from the shapes alone?

choices.text: Which region has the most orders
choices.why: A triangle is not more than a circle, so the shapes cannot say which is largest.

choices.text: The amounts, roughly, if the legend is read
choices.why: The legend would only say which shape is which region. The amounts would have to come from another channel.

choices.text: The order of the regions, but not the amounts
choices.why: That is what lightness keeps. Shape does not even keep the order.

choices.text: Which region is which, and nothing more
choices.why: Right. Shape separates categories and has no order, so it cannot carry the number.

prompt: Which of these is a category rather than a quantity?

choices.text: Delivery time in minutes
choices.why: Minutes have an amount: forty is twice twenty.

choices.text: Basket value in reais
choices.why: Money is a quantity; one basket can cost twice another.

choices.text: Payment method
choices.why: Right. Pix, card and cash are different, and none is more than another.

choices.text: Distance driven
choices.why: Kilometres are a quantity, with equal gaps between equal steps.

prompt: Five product lines are drawn as five shades of one blue, from pale to dark. What will a reader tend to do?

choices.text: Tell the lines apart easily
choices.why: Five close shades of one hue are hard to tell apart, and they also imply an order.

choices.text: Ignore the colours and read only the labels
choices.why: Readers read colour first; it is the reason for using it.

choices.text: Look for an order, and read the darkest line as the most important
choices.why: Right. Lightness has an order, so it suggests one even where the categories have none.

choices.text: Assume the lines are unrelated
choices.why: One hue in five shades says the opposite: that they belong together, in a sequence.

prompt: Which channel can carry a quantity, if only roughly, and still keep its order?

choices.text: Lightness
choices.why: Right. Anyone can sort shades from pale to dark, though nobody can read their ratios.

choices.text: Hue
choices.why: Hue has no order. It separates categories.

choices.text: Shape
choices.why: Shape has no order either.

choices.text: Texture or pattern
choices.why: A pattern can separate a few categories, but no two readers would agree on an order of patterns.

prompt: Which of these channels can separate categories? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Area
choices.why: Area carries an amount, poorly, and does not tell categories apart.

choices.text: Position on a common scale
choices.why: Right. A bar's place in the column, or a dot's place in a row, says which category it is.

choices.text: Shape
choices.why: Right, for a handful of categories.

choices.text: Hue
choices.why: Right. Telling categories apart is what hue is for.

prompt: Why does the course install matplotlib into a virtual environment rather than with sudo pip?

choices.text: Virtual environments draw charts faster than the system Python does
choices.why: Speed is the same; the point is isolation.

choices.text: matplotlib only works inside a virtual environment
choices.why: It works in any Python it is installed in. The environment is about not disturbing the system's.

choices.text: sudo pip needs a paid licence
choices.why: Nothing here costs money.

choices.text: It leaves the system's own Python untouched
choices.why: Right. Recent Linux systems refuse pip into the system Python for exactly this reason.

prompt: What is the oldest minor version of Python 3 that this course's pinned packages accept? Answer with the number after the 3, such as 9 for 3.9.
bars.py prints the five totals before drawing them. What is that habit for?

choices.text: matplotlib needs the numbers printed before it can draw them
choices.why: Drawing and printing are independent; the chart would draw without the print.

choices.text: To make the program run faster
choices.why: Printing costs a little time; it is done for the reader, not for speed.

choices.text: So the chart can be drawn from the terminal output later
choices.why: The chart is drawn from the totals in memory, in the same run.

choices.text: To notice when the chart is wrong, by comparing it with the numbers
choices.why: Right. A chart that disagrees with its own printed numbers has a bug you can see.

prompt: python3 bars.py stops with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'matplotlib', but you installed it a minute ago. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The installation failed silently
choices.why: Asking .venv/bin/python for matplotlib.__version__ would answer that, and here it answered 3.11.2.

choices.text: The program ran in the system's Python, not the environment's
choices.why: Right. Run it as .venv/bin/python bars.py.

choices.text: bars.py has a typo in its import line
choices.why: A typo would name a different module in the message. This one names matplotlib exactly.

choices.text: The CSV file is missing
choices.why: That fails later, with a different message about monthly.csv.

prompt: Python prints a long error with many lines. Where is the line that names the problem?

choices.text: At the bottom
choices.why: Right. The lines above it are the chain of calls that led there.

choices.text: At the top
choices.why: The top says a traceback follows. The problem is named last.

choices.text: In the middle, after the file name
choices.why: The middle lines say where the program was, not what went wrong.

choices.text: It is not printed; you have to run the program again with a flag
choices.why: Python always prints the error's name and message on the last line.

right_distractors: a quantity and its category at once

prompt: A dashboard colours each of Brazil's 27 states by its number of orders, using a rainbow from red to purple. Which change fixes the encoding?

choices.text: Use one hue going from pale to dark
choices.why: Right. A quantity needs an ordered channel, and lightness has an order where hue has none.

choices.text: Add a legend that explains the rainbow
choices.why: A legend helps, but every reading still goes through it, and readers misread it.

choices.text: Use more colours, one per state
choices.why: Twenty-seven hues would separate the states and say even less about which has more orders.

choices.text: Draw state borders in a thicker line
choices.why: Borders help separate the shapes, but the colour channel is the problem.
